items.title: 31.5 Fractional Distillation and Refining of Petroleum

source_refs.note: Topic 31.5 with Figure 31.6 (redrawn), its labels as a table, and Quick Check 31.3 as printed (PDF 225-226).

blocks.text: Crude oil is a complicated mixture of hydrocarbons and it needs separation into simpler and useful hydrocarbons. This separation process is done physically by a method known as fractional distillation which depends on the difference in boiling points of different hydrocarbons. During this process, the crude oil is heated inside a furnace until it is vaporized. The vapor is then passed to a fractionating column, a tall tower through which the temperature drops slowly going up.

Since the vapor travels upwards, various hydrocarbon constituents condense at various points in the column based on their boiling points. Hydrocarbons that are heavier have higher boiling point are condensed closer to the bottom, whereas lighter hydrocarbons with low boiling point rises further. The process enables the extraction of useful fractions of crude oil which are given below with their uses in Figure 31.6.

blocks.alt: A fractionating column, hottest at the bottom, fed with hot vaporized crude oil from a furnace, with a temperature bar from <20 C at the top to >370 C at the bottom and six outlets to labelled fractions, each with a picture of its uses.
blocks.caption: Figure 31.6: Fractional distillation of crude oil into useful hydrocarbons (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 31.6).
blocks.long_description: A tall fractionating column, hottest (red) at the bottom and coolest (pale yellow) at the top, with trays, upward blue arrows for rising vapour and downward arrows for falling liquid; a pipe runs from the top of the column to the gases box, its arrow pointing back towards the column. Left: a temperature bar from less than 20 C at the top to more than 370 C at the bottom; crude oil input passes through a furnace and enters the column as hot vaporized crude oil. Six outlets lead to boxes: top of the column, Gases (e.g., LPG) <25 C, cooking and heating; Gasoline (petrol) C8H18, <40 C - 200 C, fuel for cars and bikes; Kerosene C10H14, 150-275 C, jet fuel, lamps; Diesel C14-C19, 250-350 C, trucks, buses, generators; Lubricating oils C15-C20, 300-370 C, engine oil, grease; Residue (bitumen) C20+, >370 C, road surfacing, roofing. On the left of each box a car (petrol), a bus (diesel) or a ball-and-stick molecule sits above the formula; on the right the uses are drawn: gas stove and cylinder; motorbikes; airliner and lantern; bus and generator; engine and grease gun; road roller and roofing.

blocks.text: Fractional distillation is an important process as it provides petrochemicals having applications in industries, domestic, and transportation purposes.

blocks.prompt: a) If fossil fuels are non-renewable resources, why are they still heavily used worldwide?
blocks.explanation: They are very good energy sources with a high energy density, they are readily available, and vehicles, power stations and industries are built to use them; they also supply the raw materials for petrochemicals.

blocks.prompt: b) Can XRD be used to find the structure of liquid?
blocks.explanation: Not in the same way. XRD depends on the regular, repeating arrangement of atoms in a crystal. A liquid has no such long-range order, so it gives only broad, blurred patterns; usually the substance is first crystallised.
